answer:
People at Enron reacted to the 14 August 2001 resignation with surprise and sadness, many personal goodbye notes, and quick reassurance that business would go on. A few people reacted with worry about the market or about accounting. The mail also holds forwarded press coverage from that evening.

**What the announcement said.**
- The company-wide "Organizational Announcement" said the Board had accepted Skilling's resignation as President and CEO for "personal reasons", and that his decision was voluntary. Lay, as chairman, took the CEO role back.
- Lay also said he had "never felt better about the prospects for the company."
- Colleagues forwarded the announcement the same day. One example is Gerald Nemec's "Fyi".

**Surprise and "business as usual."**
- Tim Belden and Chris Calger wrote to the Portland team. They called the resignation "a surprise and generally sad news" but said the Portland business "will not be affected". They summed it up as "business as usual!"
- Vince Kaminski put off outside meetings. He wrote that the CEO "resigned today and Greg will be tied up in analyst calls for the next few days."
- Another employee wrote that there was "too much going on today with the Jeff Skilling resigning."

**Personal goodbyes to Skilling.** Many staff wrote to him directly.
- An analyst, Tim Ng, wrote "I'm sorry to hear you leave but I know you have your reasons."
- Another employee was "deeply saddened by this news that you are leaving, but can not help but feel happy for you."
- Internal Communications manager Sarah Palmer wrote "There have been a few tears shed today, and I'll admit, a couple of them were mine."
- Her director, Mary Clark, wrote "you will be missed by many, many people here at Enron."
- Rex Shelby wrote "I will miss your leadership here at Enron."

**Market worry and speculation.**
- A trader wrote that "the market here for tomorrow's close is 36 at 38". In the quoted reply, a colleague said "I hope the market doesn't hate that news."
- Elizabeth Sager asked a friend whether "Martin's retirement speech" had any impact. The email doesn't say what she meant.
- Chris Dorland sent a terse note. "The patented move is starting to pay. This just in. Skilling resigns for personal reasons. Wow!" The email doesn't explain what "the move" refers to.

**An internal concern about accounting.** Sherron Watkins, a vice president, wrote to Rick Buy that day. The email was sent only to him. She hoped Enron would "make good use of the bad news about Skilling's resignation and do some house cleaning", and asked to "write down some problem assets and unwind raptor". She said she'd been "horribly uncomfortable about some of our accounting" and feared "some disgruntled employee will tattle." Her email shows one insider linking the resignation to accounting concerns. I found no other email from that day making that link.

**Outside reaction, mostly the next day.**
- On 15 August, Robert Zoellick (USTR address) wrote to Skilling. He was "very sorry to read about your decision to leave Enron."
- David Aronoff of Greylock Partners offered to talk about Skilling's future plans.
- A family member (tskilling@tribune.com) wrote that "I'm in your corner all the way."

**Press, forwarded into the mailboxes.**
- The AP and Bloomberg wires reported that Enron shares fell 5 percent in after-hours trading, to $40.50.
- Bloomberg quoted an analyst who said "there is no immediate, capable, hands-on replacement for the likes of Jeffrey Skilling."
- The Los Angeles Times reported that his refusal to explain "prompt[ed] analysts to ask whether another shoe might drop."

**Volume.** In mail_counts, emails mentioning "Skilling" rose from 30 in the week ending 12 August to 63 in the week ending 19 August. They fell back to 31 the week after.

My searches returned a sample, not every email from that day, so this isn't a complete tally of reactions.

NEW YORK (AP) - After less than a year at the helm of energy giant Enron Corp., president and chief executive Jeffrey K. Skilling unexpectedly resigned Tuesday, citing personal reasons. 
Chairman Kenneth Lay will take over both positions, the Houston-based company said in a statement.
"I am resigning for personal reasons. I want to thank Ken Lay for his understanding of this purely personal decision, and I want to thank the board and all of my colleagues at Enron," said Skilling, who replaced Lay as CEO in February. 
"We regret Jeff's decision to resign, as he has been a big part of our success for over eleven years," said Lay. 
Enron, which earned dlrs 979 million on revenue of dlrs 100.79 billion in 2000, owns a 25,000-mile (40,000-kilometer) gas pipeline and merchant power plants in the United States and abroad producing 9,000 megawatts of electricity. 
The company has shed many energy assets, including the unit devoted to natural gas and crude oil drilling, now called EOG Resources Inc., to pursue its goal of becoming the industry's premier middleman, bringing together buyers and sellers of energy products. The company also trades metals, paper and fiber-optic bandwidth. 
Skilling will continue to work as a consultant for the Houston-based natural gas and power marketing company. 
Lay, who was Enron's CEO from 1985 until Feburary 2001, has also agreed to continue working for the company through 2005. 
Shares of Enron were off dlrs 2.43, or 5 percent, to dlrs 40.50, in after-hours trading after finishing the regular session on the New York Stock Exchange up 78 cents to dlrs 42.93.

Houston, Aug. 14 (Bloomberg) -- Enron's Jeffrey Skilling, who
became the company's chief executive in February, resigned for
personal reasons, the company said.
     Skilling, who joined the company in August 1990, was
president of the company when he was named chief executive in
December. He took over as CEO, replacing Kenneth Lay, in February.
    Lay, now Enron's chairman, will assume Skilling's duties,
Enron said in a statement. Lay's employment contract will be
extended until 2005. The company didn't immediately comment on
what led Skilling to quit.
     ``We regret Jeff's decision to resign, as he has been a big
part of our success for over 11 years,'' Lay said in a statement.
``But we have the strongest and deepest talent we have ever had in
the organization, our business is extremely strong and our growth
prospects have never been better.''
     Lay and Skilling transformed Enron from a natural-gas
pipeline company into the largest competitor in energy trading, a
business made possible by deregulation of gas and electricity
markets in the mid and late 1990s.
     Skilling has predicted that Enron will surpass $200 billion
revenue this year, making it the second-biggest U.S. energy
company behind ExxonMobil Corp.
     Though revenues have surged, profit margins have been weak
and the company hasn't been popular with investors, analysts say.
     ``If you look at the stock perform since he's taken over,
it's been pretty dismal,'' said Andre Meade, analyst with
Commerzbank Capital Markets. ``I assume he's been under some
pressure just based on share performance.''
      Enron will find it difficult to find someone who can take
over for Skilling, analysts said.
     ``My hunch is there is no immediate, capable, hands-on
replacement for the likes of Jeffrey Skilling,'' said Bob
Christensen, an analyst with First Albany Corp.
